newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tells 50 prosecutors about FBI lab problems.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tells 50 prosecutors about FBI lab problems.

text.p: The Justice Department has told about 50 prosecutors nationwide about problems at the FBI crime laboratory that could affect their cases, Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick said Thursday.

"We have, over the course of this investigation, informed about 50 prosecutors -- about half of them state or local prosecutors -- of issues relating to their cases," she said at the weekly Justice Department news briefing.

An investigation by the department's inspector general has sharply criticised the laboratory for poor management practices and sloppy handling of evidence. It has rasied questions about procedures and contaminated evidence.
The investigation began in late 1995 and produced a secret draft report last month. A final report is not expected until March at the earliest.
Gorelick's comments were the first by a department official discussing how many cases already have been affected.
She said the continuing review might add to the number of cases, and added it remained too soon to say whether any high-profile criminal prosecutions would be jeopardised.

"I tkink that we will successfully pursue the avenues available to us to address the problems that are raised by the report," she said. "We are just going to have to see how each court reacts to each separate fact pattern, as presented."
Prosecutors were notified because they must disclose to defence attorneys any evidence that may clear the defendant.

The laboratory controversy erupted after the FBI last month removed four officials from the unit in response to the investigation, including whistleblower Frederic Whitehurst whose initial complaints triggered the inquiry.

Asked if the laboratory problems would complicate the prosecution of Oklahoma City bombing suspect Timothy McVeigh, Gorelick said, "We're just going to answer every one of their motions...in court, and every one of their contentions...in court."
